newsitem.title: zaire: Rebels take Zaire capital, Kabila claims power. [CORRECTED 09:49 GMT 18/5]
newsitem.headline: Rebels take Zaire capital, Kabila claims power. [CORRECTED 09:49 GMT 18/5]

text.p: Zaire's rebels marched into the capital Kinshasa virtually unopposed on Saturday and their leader Laurent Kabila proclaimed himself head of state, crowning seven months of civil war with victory.

As jubilant crowds turned out to greet the rebels after their marathon march across Africa's third largest country, ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko's rag-tag army switched sides, ditched their uniforms or fled.
In the capital's wealthy Binza district, witnesses reported looting by residents from a neighbouring shantytown ahead of the arrival of the rebels.

Mobutu was at his jungle palace and ancestral home of Gbadolite in northern Zaire and was widely expected to join fleeing members of his family in exile, but Switzerland blocked all assets that they might hold in its banks and on its territory.
Kabila, in a statement read at a news conference in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi, said he was taking over as head of state with the agreement of generals in Kinshasa.
"According to reports from the generals, everyone was ready to take orders from me," he said, one day after Mobutu left Kinshasa for Gbadolite. One aide said Mobutu was still there on Saturday.

"Mr Laurent Desire Kabila assumes from today the functions of the head of state of the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the statement from Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) said.

Kabila has rebaptised Zaire, reverting to the title used from 1964 until Mobutu renamed the sprawling, mineral-rich country in 1971 (corrects from "...the title used after independence from Belgium in 1960 before Mobutu renamed...").
Mobutu's emergency rule prime minister, General Likulia Bolongo, called on all fighting army units to return to their barracks in a statement on state radio.

Towards the end of the day, a column of about 200 troops, some carrying weapons or a pack on their heads, entered the city centre along the "beach" road by the Zaire River, where ferries ply between Kinshasa and Congo's capital Brazzaville.
People in the crowd, waving green branches stripped from plants as a symbol of freedom, rushed to hug and touch the soldiers, thanking them as "liberators".
The main rebel force was setting up camp at the Chinese-built football stadium, where about 1,000 men including Kabila's son, Joseph, had assembled by late afternoon.

Earlier, sporadic shooting rang out in parts of the usually bustling city of five million people but France, one of five Western nations with troops across the river in Congo, said there were no plans to evacuate foreign nationals.
Rebels later entered the radio station unopposed, witnesses said. The radio told the nation to expect a message from Kabila.
Earlier, a diplomat said presidential guards from Mobutu's Nbgandi tribe had killed defence minister and army chief of staff General Mahele Lieko Bokungo.
Diplomats said Mahele, killed in Kinshasa on Friday night, had been planning to meet Kabila to discuss handing over power.
Mobutu's son, Kongolo, a presidential guard captain, fled across the Zaire River to Brazzaville, capital of Congo, on board a speedboat with about 20 other men, witnesses said.
A source at the presidency in Kinshasa and other sources in the city said that members of Mobutu's armed forces were fleeing west on the road out of the city to lower Zaire.
Kabila, 56, and his rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis.
Kabila, who has opposed Mobutu for more than 30 years, said he would set up a transitional government of public salvation within 72 hours and told Mobutu's army to lay down its arms.

He also pledged a constituent assembly within 60 days to work out a new transitional constitution, to replace the one agreed after a reluctant Mobutu bowed to foreign and domestic pressure for multi-party politics in 1990.

The United States, United Nations and South Africa's President Nelson Mandela, who have been trying to broker a peaceful transition, maintained diplomatic pressure on Kabila for a broad-based transitional authority and elections.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told a Moscow news conference that mediators remained hopeful they could persuade Kabila to form a broad-based government.
"Once that is done, there will be time to prepare national elections," he said, stressing his hope that the "choice and the voice" of the Zairean people would be respected.

Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, is suffering from cancer. Now 66, he is reputed to have amassed a huge personal fortune over the years. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.

Characteristically defiant, he did not resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila, but his abrupt departure triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile. Diplomats said Morocco or France were likely destinations.
